content: H7N3 is a subtype of the Influenza A virus, commonly referred to as a bird flu virus. In February 2004, the presence of H7N3 was confirmed at multiple poultry farms in British Columbia, Canada. By April 2004, 18 farms in the region had been placed under quarantine to prevent further spread of the virus. Two human cases of H7N3 infection were reported in the area, with symptoms including conjunctivitis and mild influenza-like illness. Both individuals made a full recovery. The H7N3 strain was first identified in turkeys in Britain in 1963. One of its more recent documented occurrences in poultry was in Canada during April and May 2004, as reported by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the World Organisation for Animal Health. In 2004, Taiwan experienced an outbreak of a less virulent bird flu strain, H5N2, which necessitated the culling of hundreds of thousands of birds. Later, in November 2005, Taiwan detected a highly pathogenic strain of H7N3 in droppings from a migratory bird. Authorities conducted tests to determine whether the virus had spread to nearby poultry farms. In April 2006, H7N3 was identified in the United Kingdom for the first time since 1979. The outbreak occurred at Witford Lodge Farm in Norfolk, England, where the virus infected birds and one poultry worker. The worker's only symptom was conjunctivitis. As a precaution, antiviral medication (Tamiflu) was administered to poultry workers at the farm. To contain the outbreak, 35,000 chickens were culled, and a 1-kilometer exclusion zone was established around the infected farm. On September 27, 2007, another outbreak of H7N3 was reported at a poultry operation in Saskatchewan, Canada. The Canadian Food Inspection Agency ordered the euthanization of the affected flock and mandated the disinfection of all buildings, materials, and equipment that had come into contact with the birds or their droppings.
